title: The son who left (Luke 15:11–24)
hook: the younger son spends it all, comes to himself, and the father runs down the road

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lost sheep and the lost coin. Your line was he goes looking. Did you reach out to someone who drifted? Day forty-seven. Today, the third story of losing, and the most famous.

A man has two sons. The younger one comes to him and says: give me my share of the inheritance. Now. Not when you die. Now. In that world, and in most of ours, that's close to saying: I wish you were already gone. And the father does it. He divides his property, and the younger son sells up, packs everything, and leaves for a far country. There he wastes it all, living wildly. Then a famine hits the land. He takes the only job he can find, feeding pigs, and he's so hungry he'd gladly eat what the pigs are eating. Nobody gives him anything. Today: the son who left, and what happened when he turned around.
screen: `GIVE ME MY SHARE. NOW.` → `A FAR COUNTRY, AND A FAMINE.` → `FEEDING PIGS, STARVING.`

segments.voice: Then comes a small phrase with a lot inside it. The Douay-Rheims says: returning to himself. The King James says he came to himself. As if he'd been away from himself, too. He does the math. My father's hired workers have more bread than they need, and I'm dying of hunger. So he writes a speech in his head: "I will arise, and will go to my father." He'll say: I've sinned against heaven and before you. I'm not worthy to be called your son. Make me one of your hired workers. He's not hoping to be a son again. He's hoping for a job. And he starts the long walk home. Now watch the father. "And when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and running to him fell upon his neck, and kissed him." He saw him a great way off. Which means he'd been watching the road. And he runs. In that culture, a dignified older man didn't run. He'd have to hitch up his robe and show his legs. The father doesn't care. He reaches his son before the son can reach the village. The son starts his speech, and the father doesn't even let him get to the part about the hired workers. Bring the best robe. A ring for his hand. Shoes for his feet. Kill the fatted calf. "Because this my son was dead, and is come to life again: was lost, and is found." Catholics hear this story as the heart of the sacrament of confession: you come with your speech, and the Father runs to meet you. Pope John Paul the Second built a whole letter on mercy around it.
screen: `RETURNING TO HIMSELF.` · `A SPEECH ASKING FOR A JOB.` · `A GREAT WAY OFF, THE FATHER RUNS.` · `THE ROBE, THE RING, THE CALF.` · then, large: `WAS LOST, AND IS FOUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one step back toward someone. Settle and breathe. Think of a relationship where there's distance you helped make. Maybe you left. Maybe you said something. Maybe you just went quiet. You don't have to walk the whole road today. Just picture the first step: a message, a call, an honest sentence. If you pray, you can bring your own speech to God and notice that you don't have to finish it. The bell holds the time.
The son who left. He wasted everything, came to himself, and walked home hoping for a job, and his father ran to meet him. Today's word.
Your line: the father runs. Today, take one step back toward someone. The story says the distance is shorter than it looks. Day forty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the parable of the prodigal son in Lent and often in preparing for confession, where the penitent comes back and receives absolution; John Paul II's encyclical Dives in Misericordia (1980) meditates on it at length.

fork.setup: you're the father. far down the road you see the son who took half your fortune and left. what do you do?

run down the road to meet him.

original.note: Greek: wastefully, recklessly; the word behind living riotously. The son's life in the far country.

trapdoor: what you thought: a son wastes his money and comes home sorry.
what it means: a son comes back hoping for a job, and a father who had been watching the road runs to give him back his place.
what a scholar hears: a dignified father running was shocking in that culture. the Church hears in it the heart of confession.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 15:18, 15:20, 15:24 given from memory; confirm. 'Returning to himself' (15:17) is also Douay-Rheims.
Asking for the inheritance early as close to wishing the father dead, and an older man running as undignified, are common readings (e.g. Kenneth Bailey); presented as cultural background. Confirm.
Dives in Misericordia (1980), sections 5–6, meditate on the parable; confirm.
The link to the sacrament of confession is a common Catholic reading; confirm phrasing.
